title: Inferno, Canto I
author: Dante Alighieri
source_notes: Italian text follows the standard Petrocchi edition. English: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's terza rima translation, 1867 (public domain).
reading_notes: The opening canto of the Commedia. Dante, lost in a dark wood at midlife, sees a sunlit hill, attempts to climb it, and is driven back by three beasts: a leopard (lonza), a lion (leone), and a she-wolf (lupa). Virgil appears and offers to lead him through Hell. Lines 1–60 — the canonical opening of the poem and one of the most famous beginnings in world literature.

lines.original: Nel mezzo del cammin di nostra vita
lines.english: Midway upon the journey of our life
lines.gloss: *nel mezzo* (in the middle) + *del cammin* (of the journey, *cammino* with apocope) + *di nostra vita* (of our life). 'Cammin' = path, journey; the first-person 'nostra' makes the experience universal, not merely personal.

lines.original: mi ritrovai per una selva oscura,
lines.english: I found myself within a forest dark,
lines.gloss: *mi ritrovai* (I found myself; reflexive past absolute) + *per una selva oscura* (in/through a dark wood). 'Ritrovarsi' suggests sudden self-awareness, not deliberate arrival. 'Selva' = forest; 'oscura' = dark, obscure, morally clouded.

lines.original: ché la diritta via era smarrita.
lines.english: For the straightforward pathway had been lost.
lines.gloss: *ché* (because, since; conjunction) + *la diritta via* (the straight road) + *era smarrita* (was lost; passive). 'Smarrita' carries both spatial and moral senses — bewildered, gone astray. The 'diritta via' is the path of righteousness.

lines.original: Ahi quanto a dir qual era è cosa dura
lines.english: Ah me! how hard a thing it is to say
lines.gloss: *Ahi* (interjection of pain) + *quanto a dir* (how much to say) + *qual era* (what it was) + *è cosa dura* (is a hard thing). The poet pauses to mark the difficulty of describing the wood.

lines.original: esta selva selvaggia e aspra e forte
lines.english: What was this forest savage, rough, and stern,
lines.gloss: *esta* (this; archaic for *questa*) + *selva selvaggia* (savage forest; etymological play, *selva/selvaggia* both from Latin *silva*) + *aspra* (rough) + *forte* (harsh, dense). The triple adjective is a Trecento rhetorical figure.

lines.original: che nel pensier rinova la paura!
lines.english: Which in the very thought renews the fear.
lines.gloss: *che* (which) + *nel pensier* (in the thought, *pensiero* with apocope) + *rinova* (renews; *rinnova*) + *la paura* (the fear). The mere memory recreates the terror.

lines.original: Tant'è amara che poco è più morte;
lines.english: So bitter is it, death is little more;
lines.gloss: *Tant'è amara* (so bitter is it) + *che poco è più* (that little more is) + *morte* (death). The taste of the wood approaches the taste of death itself.

lines.original: ma per trattar del ben ch'i' vi trovai,
lines.english: But of the good to treat, which there I found,
lines.gloss: *ma per trattar* (but to treat of) + *del ben* (of the good) + *ch'i' vi trovai* (which I found there; *i'* = *io*). Despite the horror, Dante found something good — the encounter to come.

lines.original: dirò de l'altre cose ch'i' v'ho scorte.
lines.english: Speak will I of the other things I saw there.
lines.gloss: *dirò* (I will tell; future of *dire*) + *de l'altre cose* (of the other things) + *ch'i' v'ho scorte* (which I have glimpsed there; *scorgere* = to perceive, with the subject 'i' = io).

lines.original: Io non so ben ridir com'i' v'intrai,
lines.english: I cannot well repeat how there I entered,
lines.gloss: *Io non so ben ridir* (I do not know well how to retell) + *com'i' v'intrai* (how I entered there; *intrai* archaic past absolute of *entrare*). The poet cannot reconstruct his fall into the wood.

lines.original: tant'era pien di sonno a quel punto
lines.english: So full was I of slumber at the moment
lines.gloss: *tant'era pien di sonno* (so full was I of sleep) + *a quel punto* (at that point/moment). 'Sonno' here is moral drowsiness, not literal sleep — the soul's torpor.

lines.original: che la verace via abbandonai.
lines.english: In which I had abandoned the true way.
lines.gloss: *che* (in which) + *la verace via* (the true way) + *abbandonai* (I abandoned; past absolute of *abbandonare*). The 'verace via' contrasts with the 'diritta via' of line 3 — both are the way of truth.

lines.original: Ma poi ch'i' fui al piè d'un colle giunto,
lines.english: But after I had reached a mountain's foot,
lines.gloss: *Ma poi ch'i' fui* (but after I was) + *al piè d'un colle* (at the foot of a hill, *piede* with apocope) + *giunto* (arrived; past participle of *giungere*). The first turn of fortune in the canto.

lines.original: là dove terminava quella valle
lines.english: At that point where the valley terminated,
lines.gloss: *là dove* (there where) + *terminava* (was ending; imperfect of *terminare*) + *quella valle* (that valley). The wood is a valley; the sunlit hill rises beyond it.

lines.original: che m'avea di paura il cor compunto,
lines.english: Which had with consternation pierced my heart,
lines.gloss: *che m'avea* (which had me) + *di paura* (with fear) + *il cor compunto* (pricked the heart; *compunto* = pierced, *cor* archaic for *cuore*). The valley had pierced his heart with fear.

lines.original: guardai in alto e vidi le sue spalle
lines.english: Upward I looked, and I beheld its shoulders,
lines.gloss: *guardai in alto* (I looked upward; past absolute of *guardare*) + *e vidi le sue spalle* (and saw its shoulders; the hill's). 'Spalle' = shoulders, sides of the hill.

lines.original: vestite già de' raggi del pianeta
lines.english: Vested already with that planet's rays
lines.gloss: *vestite* (clothed; past part. of *vestire*, agreeing with *spalle*) + *già de' raggi* (already with the rays, *de'* = *dei*) + *del pianeta* (of the planet). The 'pianeta' is the sun, in medieval cosmology.

lines.original: che mena dritto altrui per ogne calle.
lines.english: Which leadeth others right by every road.
lines.gloss: *che mena* (which leads) + *dritto* (straight) + *altrui* (others) + *per ogne calle* (along every path; *ogne* = *ogni*; *calle* = lane, way). The sun, in Dante, is the figure of grace and right reason.

lines.original: Allor fu la paura un poco queta,
lines.english: Then was the fear a little quieted
lines.gloss: *Allor* (then; *allora*) + *fu* (was) + *la paura* (the fear) + *un poco queta* (a little quieted). The hill's light calms the wood's terror.

lines.original: che nel lago del cor m'era durata
lines.english: That in my heart's lake had endured throughout
lines.gloss: *che nel lago del cor* (which in the lake of the heart) + *m'era durata* (had endured for me; pluperfect of *durare*). The 'lago del cor' is the chamber of the heart in medieval physiology.

lines.original: la notte ch'i' passai con tanta pieta.
lines.english: The night, which I had passed so piteously.
lines.gloss: *la notte* (the night) + *ch'i' passai* (which I passed; past absolute) + *con tanta pieta* (with such pity, *pieta* = *pietà*). The night just survived was a night of dread.

lines.original: E come quei che con lena affannata,
lines.english: And even as he, who, with distressful breath,
lines.gloss: *E come quei* (and like the one) + *che con lena affannata* (who with breathless effort, *lena* = breath, energy). The simile: like a man saved from drowning.

lines.original: uscito fuor del pelago a la riva,
lines.english: Forth issued from the sea upon the shore,
lines.gloss: *uscito fuor* (come out; past part. of *uscire*) + *del pelago* (from the sea, *pelago* = open sea) + *a la riva* (to the shore). The image of escape from drowning.

lines.original: si volge a l'acqua perigliosa e guata,
lines.english: Turns to the water perilous and gazes;
lines.gloss: *si volge* (turns himself; reflexive of *volgere*) + *a l'acqua perigliosa* (to the perilous water) + *e guata* (and gazes; *guatare* = to look intently). The survivor looks back at what he escaped.

lines.original: così l'animo mio, ch'ancor fuggiva,
lines.english: So did my soul, that still was fleeing onward,
lines.gloss: *così l'animo mio* (so my soul) + *ch'ancor fuggiva* (which still was fleeing; imperfect of *fuggire*). The simile resolves: Dante's soul, still in flight, turns to look at the wood.

lines.original: si volse a retro a rimirar lo passo
lines.english: Turn itself back to re-behold the pass
lines.gloss: *si volse a retro* (turned itself backward; *a retro* = back) + *a rimirar* (to gaze upon again; *rimirare*) + *lo passo* (the passage). The reflexive verb echoes line 24.

lines.original: che non lasciò già mai persona viva.
lines.english: Which never yet a living person left.
lines.gloss: *che non lasciò* (which never let; past absolute of *lasciare*) + *già mai* (ever) + *persona viva* (a living person). No living person had ever come out of that 'passo' alive — it is hell's threshold.

lines.original: Poi ch'èi posato un poco il corpo lasso,
lines.english: After my weary body I had rested,
lines.gloss: *Poi ch'èi* (after I had; *èi* = *ebbi* of *avere*) + *posato* (rested) + *un poco il corpo lasso* (a little the weary body, *lasso* = exhausted). 'Lasso' is also a poetic exclamation of grief.

lines.original: ripresi via per la piaggia diserta,
lines.english: The way resumed I o'er the desert slope,
lines.gloss: *ripresi via* (I took up the way again; past absolute of *riprendere*) + *per la piaggia diserta* (along the desert slope, *piaggia* = slope/strand).

lines.original: sì che 'l piè fermo sempre era 'l più basso.
lines.english: So that the firm foot ever was the lower.
lines.gloss: *sì che 'l piè fermo* (so that the firm foot, *'l* = *il*) + *sempre era 'l più basso* (was always the lower). A famous crux: climbing uphill, the standing foot stays planted lower than the moving foot. Many readers see in this an allegory of moral progress.

lines.original: Ed ecco, quasi al cominciar de l'erta,
lines.english: And lo! almost where the ascent began,
lines.gloss: *Ed ecco* (and behold) + *quasi al cominciar* (almost at the beginning) + *de l'erta* (of the steep ascent, *erta* = steep slope). The first beast appears.

lines.original: una lonza leggera e presta molto,
lines.english: A panther, light and swift exceedingly,
lines.gloss: *una lonza* (a leopard or lynx; medieval Italian for a spotted feline) + *leggera* (light, nimble) + *e presta molto* (and very ready/quick). The lonza is traditionally read as the sin of lust.

lines.original: che di pel macolato era coverta;
lines.english: Which with a spotted skin was covered o'er!
lines.gloss: *che di pel macolato* (which with spotted hide; *macolato* = *macchiato*) + *era coverta* (was covered; *coperta*). The spotted coat itself becomes an emblem of confusion and desire.

lines.original: E non mi si partia dinanzi al volto,
lines.english: And never moved she from before my face,
lines.gloss: *E non mi si partia* (and would not depart from me; imperfect reflexive of *partirsi*) + *dinanzi al volto* (in front of my face). The leopard blocks the path.

lines.original: anzi 'mpediva tanto il mio cammino,
lines.english: Nay, rather did impede so much my way,
lines.gloss: *anzi* (rather, on the contrary) + *'mpediva tanto* (was so impeding; *impediva* with aphesis) + *il mio cammino* (my way).

lines.original: ch'i' fui per ritornar più volte vòlto.
lines.english: That many times I to return had turned.
lines.gloss: *ch'i' fui* (that I was) + *per ritornar* (about to turn back) + *più volte vòlto* (turned many times). 'Vòlto' (turned) puns on 'volto' (face) of line 34. The pilgrim is on the verge of giving up.
